claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in the stated starting condition has favorable plasticity and machinability but relatively low hardness and strength.
Weak grain boundaries caused by Ti segregation govern the low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Ti segregation promotes early intergranular plasticity in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Ti enrichment at grain boundaries reduces dislocation storage within the grains.
Ti enrichment at grain boundaries facilitates grain-boundary sliding or decohesion.
The applicable starting material is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a single-phase solid-solution state.
Some Ti segregation at grain boundaries is expected after conventional casting or annealing of this alloy.
Controlled heat treatment or rapid solidification can be used to accentuate or suppress grain-boundary Ti segregation.
Grain-boundary Ti enrichment mediates the balance between intragranular dislocation motion and grain-boundary-controlled deformation.
Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has limited lattice distortion and unoptimized solid-solution strengthening.
Ti-enriched grain-boundary regions are mechanically weaker than the grain interiors or Ti-depleted boundaries.
A sample with more pronounced Ti grain-boundary segregation will have lower hardness than a sample with minimized segregation.
A sample with more pronounced Ti grain-boundary segregation will have lower yield strength than a sample with minimized segregation.
Pronounced Ti segregation will produce more evidence of grain-boundary sliding or early intergranular fracture.
Suppressing Ti grain-boundary segregation will strengthen grain-boundary interactions and favor dislocation-mediated deformation.
Nanoindentation and micro- or nanopillar compression are suitable methods for comparing the mechanical response of the two sample sets.
The proposed mechanism is bounded to single-phase equimolar CoCrFeNiTi under moderate room-temperature nanoindentation or micropillar-compression loading.
The relative contributions of grain-boundary sliding and dislocation-mediated plasticity may vary with grain size and processing conditions.
Slow cooling encourages Ti segregation, whereas rapid solidification minimizes elemental segregation in this alloy.

Failure of markedly different grain-boundary Ti levels to produce higher hardness and yield strength in the low-segregation sample, together with similar deformation modes, would falsify the proposed governing role of Ti segregation.
